entities.summary: John of Wales (John Waleys, Johannes Guallensis), a Franciscan theologian, wrote several well-received Latin works, primarily preaching aids, and played a significant role in shaping the medieval Church's theological understanding. He was born in Wales, around 1250, and died in 1285. His writings, such as the 'Summa Theologica', influenced various European scholars, including Thomas Aquinas. John of Wales' contributions to the Franciscan Order and the Church's theological discourse have endured, leaving a lasting legacy in the annals of medieval history. The Franciscan friar's writings have been preserved in several manuscripts, including the 'Codex Aureus of Lorsch', a prized manuscript now housed in the library of the University of Mainz. His work, 'De natura hominis', examined the nature of humanity and God's relationship with humans. John of Wales' theological ideas have been studied by scholars, including the 14th-century Dominican friar, Duns Scotus, who built upon his work. The theologian's writings also demonstrate his understanding of Aristotelian philosophy, as seen in his treatise 'De potentia Dei'. John of Wales' Franciscan order was instrumental in spreading the teachings of St. Francis of Assisi, and his writings played a crucial role in shaping the Church's doctrine on the poor and the marginalized. The theologian's legacy extends beyond his written works, as his teachings and writings have influenced various European monastic communities, including the Cistercian and Dominican orders. John of Wales' significance in the annals of medieval history is evident in his contributions to the development of Franciscan theology and his impact on the Church's understanding of the poor and the marginalized.
